stem: A client has clinical factors that make creatinine/cystatin C–based eGFR unreliable, and an exogenous-marker measured GFR is not available. The provider orders a timed urine collection for creatinine clearance. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Timed creatinine clearance can be used as a fallback estimate in this situation, but it is prone to collection and biologic error and is not the preferred gold-standard GFR measurement.
options.B: A 24-hour creatinine clearance is always more accurate than combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR and should replace eGFR in every client.
options.C: Timed urine creatinine clearance directly measures liver function and provides no information related to glomerular filtration.
options.D: Creatinine clearance is the gold-standard measured GFR method because endogenous creatinine has no tubular secretion and timed urine collections are essentially error-free.

rationale: KDIGO 2024 recommends serum creatinine with an estimating equation for initial GFR assessment and recommends combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR when creatinine-based eGFR is less accurate and GFR affects clinical decisions. When still greater accuracy is needed, measured GFR using plasma or urinary clearance of an exogenous filtration marker is preferred. KDIGO Practice Point 1.2.2.8 permits timed urine creatinine clearance when measured GFR is unavailable and eGFRcr-cys is thought to be inaccurate, but Table 9 characterizes timed creatinine clearance as highly prone to errors. Therefore, A is correct. B and D overstate its accuracy/status, and C misidentifies the physiologic function being assessed.
educational_objective: Understand timed urine creatinine clearance as a limited fallback method for GFR assessment when combined eGFR is unreliable and exogenous-marker measured GFR is unavailable, rather than as a universal gold standard.
source_document_title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
source_version_date: 2024; confirmed current global CKD standard in 2026
source_locator: Chapter 1, Section 1.2.2: Practice Point 1.2.2.1 — use SCr/eGFR for initial GFR assessment; Recommendation 1.2.2.1 — use eGFRcr-cys when eGFRcr is less accurate and GFR affects decisions; Practice Point 1.2.2.2 — use plasma or urinary clearance of an exogenous filtration marker when more accurate GFR ascertainment affects treatment; Practice Point 1.2.2.8 — consider timed urine creatinine clearance if mGFR is unavailable and eGFRcr-cys is thought inaccurate. Table 9 — timed urine creatinine clearance is highly prone to error and recommended only when other supportive options are unavailable.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports timed creatinine clearance as a fallback rather than preferred GFR method and identifies exogenous-marker clearance as the measured-GFR standard when greater accuracy is required.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential → Diagnostic Tests/Laboratory Procedures: understand indications and limitations of renal-function tests, support accurate specimen collection, and interpret testing methods in clinical context.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — limitations and role of timed creatinine clearance
correction_summary: Substantively corrected the source claim that 24-hour creatinine clearance may simply be 'preferred over eGFR' for extremes of body size or muscle mass. Current KDIGO first favors eGFRcr-cys when creatinine eGFR is inaccurate, then exogenous-marker measured GFR when greater accuracy is needed; timed creatinine clearance is a fallback when mGFR is unavailable and eGFRcr-cys is unreliable, and it is highly prone to error.

audit_findings.clinical_category: GFR assessment method selection and timed creatinine-clearance limitations
audit_findings.currentness: The 2024 Chapter 1 GFR evaluation framework remains current in 2026 and is outside the scope of KDIGO's focused Chapter 3 update.

claim_by_claim.stem: The scenario exactly matches Practice Point 1.2.2.8: eGFRcr-cys unreliable and mGFR unavailable.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because timed creatinine clearance is permitted as a fallback but is explicitly described as highly prone to error.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because KDIGO generally prefers eGFRcr-cys when creatinine eGFR is inaccurate and does not make timed clearance universally superior.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because creatinine clearance estimates renal clearance/GFR-related function, not liver function.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because exogenous filtration markers are the measured-GFR standard and creatinine/timed collections have known limitations.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Does not claim that timed creatinine clearance is useless; it preserves its appropriate fallback role.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to selecting/interpreting renal-function testing methods.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests universal-superiority misconception, C wrong-organ interpretation, and D falsely labels endogenous creatinine clearance as gold standard. Each is distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A matches the exact KDIGO testing hierarchy and limitations.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe the role/accuracy of the same timed creatinine-clearance test.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate because the construct is diagnostic-test selection and interpretation rather than disease pathophysiology.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited the potential statement that muscle-mass extremes automatically require 24-hour urine collection. KDIGO instead favors cystatin-C-based strategies in many such cases; the final item avoids that outdated shortcut. No unresolved conflict remains.
